Stephen Miller will take over as White House Chief of Staff Monday, replacing Suzy Wiles.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports President Trump announced the move just days after Republicans
suffered major losses in the midterm elections. Democrats are sharply criticizing Miller's
promotion as they prepared to take control of Congress. Virginia Congressman Don Beyer

force, the Darth Vader of this country right now, of this presidential leadership, what he's done
with the cruel and chaotic immigration enforcement. President Trump praised Miller at an event in
Florida. He's very loyal, smart. He does a great job. He's been an MVP every year.
Miller has been with Trump since the 2016 presidential campaign. He moves up from
Deputy Chief of Staff Wile Wiles, shifts to the administration's political operation.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News, Washington. First Lady Melania Trump is launching Fostering the Future
scholarships for students in foster care who are heading to college. There is nothing more
powerful. We can give a young person than a world class education. Speaking at Louisiana State
University in Baton Rouge, the First Lady unveiled a new multi-million dollar permanent endowment
fund through the university. It's meant to provide full scholarships for young adults who have been
through the foster care system. Thousands gathered across France for a fourth weekend of demonstrations
calling for higher wages and better conditions in the schools. As Rebecca Rosman reports, the prime
minister is expected to meet with union heads and businesses on Monday to come up with solutions
and discuss the protesters' demands. France's Interior Ministry says nearly 150,000 people
gathered across the country Saturday, a lower turnout than previous demonstrations. A nationwide
strike just two days ago drew more than half a million people. Still, the French government says
it's taking the protesters' grievances seriously. On Monday, the French prime minister will meet with
business leaders and workers to discuss wages and living conditions. The protests began in late
September as a student movement calling for better conditions in schools, but have since evolved into
a national push to address wider inequalities across French society. The demonstrations turned
violent in mid-October. Businesses were looted and set on fire, costing millions in damages.
Rebecca Rosman and Pierre Neuse, Paris. Japan's meteorological agency reports a
strong earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 5.7 that has struck central Japan. It was followed
by smaller aftershocks. Japanese media reportedly 22 people have been hurt. Authorities also say
there is no risk of a tsunami. You're listening to NPR.
Paraguay's former president has appeared before the country's prosecutors. He was earlier removed
from office, arrested, and placed under house arrest over a bank scandal. That scandal left
millions unable to access their own money. Catherine Osborne has the story from Rio de Janeiro.
Santiago Pena, impeached as Paraguay's president on Friday, was a close ally of President Trump.
He was known as a pro-market leader focused on making it easier to do business in the country.
But investigations allege he was too friendly to a large digital bank, which broke regulations
and collapsed. It left millions of people blocked from their savings and triggered street protests.
A trial is proceeding against Pena, while his former vice president Pedro Aliana was sworn in
as president. The U.S. embassy said it looks forward to working with him. For NPR News,
I'm Catherine Osborne in Rio de Janeiro. The burger chain Wendy's has been looking to sell,
but it's not jumping at just any offer. Wendy's solidly rejected a $1.4 billion
buyout offer, saying the bid was just too low. That bid from investor and former Wendy's chairman,
Nelson Peltz, made the offer last week. A committee of independent directors unanimously
rejected the bid, opting instead to hold out for a better deal. Wendy's has been struggling with
high beef prices, along with aging infrastructure affecting many of its stores. Wendy's is sometimes
remembered for the "where's the beef" catchphrase from its famous 1984 advertising campaign.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
